text: <|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>What does DocAtlas mean by treating long-document understanding as a mutable-state information-seeking process?<|assistant|>In a static retrieval system, pages are embedded into a fixed index and a top-k subset is selected before generation, so the retrieval state never changes during an episode. DocAtlas instead instantiates a mutable document harness: an external environment that determines what document information is searched, read, stored, reviewed, and shown to the model at each step. The harness exposes search, reading, note-taking, and review tools and maintains a hierarchical tree and a note store, updating both as the agent records evidence, so the state seen by later tool calls depends on earlier interactions.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>What results does DocAtlas report on MMLongBench-Doc, and what makes the compact-model result notable?<|assistant|>With GPT-5.4 as the backbone, DocAtlas reaches 71.4% on MMLongBench-Doc, exceeding the human-expert reference of 65.8%. Separately, a Qwen3.5-4B vision-language model trained with end-to-end reinforcement learning inside the DocAtlas environment reaches 63.7%, compared with a 54.4% direct-input baseline. The compact-model gain is the stronger claim, since it shows the harness design itself improves small document agents by a large margin rather than the result being carried by a very large proprietary backbone.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>Why does simply feeding an entire long document into a vision-language model fail?<|assistant|>Two separate reasons. First, long documents such as financial reports, legal contracts and government filings can run to hundreds of pages and quickly exceed the practical limits of current vision-language models. Second, even when the input does fit within the context window, performance often drops because irrelevant content competes for attention. Static retrieval only partly helps: it selects a fixed subset of pages but cannot refine its search as evidence accumulates.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>How does the DocAtlas paper distinguish the terms model, policy, and agent?<|assistant|>Model, or backbone, refers to the underlying vision-language model weights; policy refers to the mapping from interaction history to the next action; and agent refers to the policy running inside the DocAtlas tool environment. The same VLM is therefore described as a model when discussing architecture or size, as a policy when discussing reinforcement learning or action choices, and as an agent when it interacts with tools and the environment.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>How many epochs was GPT-5.4 fine-tuned for inside the DocAtlas environment to reach 71.4%?<|assistant|>GPT-5.4 was not fine-tuned at all, so there is no epoch count. The paper distinguishes two uses of the same harness: inference-time use with large VLMs, which is how the 71.4% GPT-5.4 result was obtained, and end-to-end reinforcement learning for compact VLM agents, which is how the Qwen3.5-4B model was trained to 63.7%. Only the compact model is trained in the environment.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>What is PoVisLE, and how large and how composed is the dataset?<|assistant|>PoVisLE is a monocultural vision-language benchmark for Polish, designed to evaluate culturally grounded multimodal understanding under a grounded evaluation paradigm in which language is interpreted in interaction with visual context. It contains 1,117 unique images and 2,366 manually annotated VQA pairs, an average of 2.12 questions per image. Images come mostly from Wikimedia Commons (70.28%), followed by annotator-provided images (28.74%) and other sources (0.98%).

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>How are PoVisLE's questions distributed by type, and what makes them harder than template-driven benchmarks?<|assistant|>The distribution is fairly balanced: yes/no questions account for 36.7%, multiple-choice for 36.1%, and open-ended for 27.2%. Multiple-choice items vary from 2 to 8 options with an average of 4.29. The questions average 18.7 tokens and frequently use multi-clause formulations, giving substantial linguistic diversity and structural complexity, which supports context-rich, non-template-based reasoning rather than the surface-level recognition that template-driven cultural benchmarks tend to test.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>What is circular evaluation in PoVisLE, and what problem does it solve?<|assistant|>For multiple-choice questions the answer options are cyclically permuted, so a three-option item is evaluated in the orders A,B,C then B,C,A then C,A,B, and the instance counts as correct only when the model selects the correct answer under every rotation. This reduces the effect of option-position bias, where a model favours a particular slot rather than a particular answer, while requiring far fewer evaluations than checking all possible permutations. Yes/no and open-ended questions are evaluated in a single pass instead.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>How does PoVisLE operationalize 'culture' for dataset construction?<|assistant|>Following prior work on culturally situated evaluation and the text-only PLCC benchmark, culture is operationalized as a structured combination of tangible cultural artifacts and intangible shared social practices. Poland is treated as a proxy for a culturally and linguistically coherent group, assuming a shared baseline of cultural knowledge among annotators and target users while acknowledging internal regional variation. The authors deliberately avoided centring a single urban or institutionalized perspective, which would favour capital-centric culture, and instead incorporated geographically distributed content.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>Which other Slavic languages does PoVisLE cover besides Polish, and how do their scores compare?<|assistant|>None, so there are no comparative scores. PoVisLE is explicitly a monocultural benchmark: it targets Polish language and Polish culture alone, treating Poland as a single culturally and linguistically coherent group. Extending the approach to other languages or cultures would require constructing separate datasets, since the images, questions and cultural assumptions are all Poland-specific.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>What are Prompt Embedding Probes, and how do they extend a standard linear probe?<|assistant|>PEP is a white-box method for answer-level hallucination detection that reads the hidden states of a frozen large language model. It extends the standard linear probe by augmenting the model's input with a small number of learnable prompt embeddings, so the representation being probed can itself be shaped for the detection task. The backbone stays frozen and only a small number of parameters are trainable, which keeps the method far cheaper than fine-tuning.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>How is the hallucination detection task formalised in PEP, and what distinguishes its TBG and SLT settings?<|assistant|>Given a query x and a model-generated answer a, the goal is to predict a binary label y, with y = 1 denoting a hallucinated answer; a detector is a scoring function f_theta(x, a) mapping to [0, 1]. The two settings differ in when detection happens. In the to-be-generated (TBG) setting, detection is performed before the answer is generated, which makes it a pre-generation prediction. In the second-last-token (SLT) setting, detection uses representations obtained after the answer has been processed.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>On which datasets was PEP evaluated, and why were those three chosen?<|assistant|>PEP was evaluated on TriviaQA, GSM8K and MedQA with Qwen3 models at multiple scales, because the three cover distinct answer types: TriviaQA targets short factual question answering, GSM8K focuses on mathematical reasoning, and MedQA represents a high-risk medical setting with multiple-choice answers. The splits used were 10,000/1,000/17,944 for TriviaQA, 6,473/1,000/1,319 for GSM8K, and 8,000/1,000/1,273 for MedQA. Each has a task-specific system prompt, for instance 'Answer briefly.' for TriviaQA.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>Where does PEP generalise well and where does it fall short?<|assistant|>PEP improves on standard linear probes in the main in-distribution setting, and it remains effective in two harder regimes: pre-generation prediction, where the answer does not yet exist, and cross-model transfer. Robust cross-dataset transfer, however, remains difficult. The authors also report an untuned PEP variant using a configuration fixed a priori, probing at 0.6 of total model depth with 10 prompt embeddings, alongside a tuned variant whose probing layer is selected on validation data.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>How much did fine-tuning the Qwen3 backbone during PEP training contribute to the detection gains?<|assistant|>The backbone is never fine-tuned, so the question does not apply. PEP is explicitly a method for probing a frozen LLM: the whole point of adding a small number of learnable prompt embeddings is to strengthen hidden-state probing while keeping the backbone frozen and the trainable parameter count small. Any gain reported comes from the prompt embeddings and the probe, not from updating the model.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>What is 'degenerate agreement' in on-policy distillation, and why does it make token agreement a misleading objective?<|assistant|>Degenerate agreement is a failure mode in which the student exploits repetitive loops to achieve near-perfect token agreement with the teacher while its responses are globally flawed. Because agreement is measured per token, a student that keeps repeating a locally predictable continuation scores well without producing a correct answer. The authors trace on-policy distillation's abrupt length inflation, where generations drift toward the decoding cap, to exactly these persistent repetitive loops, which is why they shift attention from agreement to teacher-student mismatch.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>What distinguishes student-excess tokens from student-deficit tokens, and what problem does each cause?<|assistant|>Student-excess tokens are generated by the student but assigned near-zero probability by the teacher; their log-ratio corrections grow unbounded and destabilize the update. Student-deficit tokens are the mirror image: preferred by the teacher but rarely sampled by the student, so they seldom appear in the on-policy trajectories at all, and their absence blocks the transfer of the teacher's reasoning patterns. One direction breaks optimization stability, the other silently withholds the knowledge being distilled.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>How does TIDE correct each of the two mismatch directions?<|assistant|>TIDE stands for Token-level Independent Deficit-Excess correction, and it treats the two directions with different mechanisms. For excesses it applies bounded Hellinger shaping to suppress the most severe sampled excesses, the boundedness being what prevents the unbounded log-ratio corrections from destabilizing training. For deficits it uses an analytic teacher top-K injection to restore deficient probability mass without requiring the deficit tokens to be sampled, which is essential because those tokens are by definition rarely produced by the student. Only positions with substantial mismatch in either direction receive corrective updates; all remaining tokens are excluded from the distillation objective.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>What gains does TIDE deliver under strong teacher-student mismatch?<|assistant|>The advantage is largest exactly where mismatch is severe. Under strong teacher-student mismatch, TIDE improves Avg@8 from 6.9% to 20.3%, reduces average response length by a factor of 3.6, and substantially reduces formatting failures. Across mathematical reasoning benchmarks with multiple Qwen3 teacher-student pairs it consistently outperforms standard on-policy distillation as well as recent token-selection and reward-shaping baselines.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>How large is the reward model that TIDE trains to score student rollouts?<|assistant|>TIDE trains no reward model, so the premise does not hold. It is an on-policy distillation method whose supervision comes from a fixed teacher's next-token distribution queried at the states the student actually visits, and its objective is the trajectory-level reverse KL divergence between student and teacher rather than a learned reward. The paper contrasts this denser token-level feedback with the sparse outcome rewards used in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, which is the setting where a reward model would appear.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>What is the analogy between an autonomous research agent and a greybox fuzzer, and what does it reveal about the generate-and-rank paradigm?<|assistant|>Within a declared research problem an agent follows the same control loop as a greybox fuzzer: propose a candidate, execute it, observe feedback, and choose what to try next. A fuzzer rarely finds a bug, but coverage makes partial progress observable on every execution, and the fuzzer uses that signal to mutate inputs and allocate effort rather than only to rank completed runs. The authors argue that the prevailing generate-and-rank response, scaling the proposer and ranking more samples with a learned judge or human reviewers, addresses the wrong bottleneck, because the real problem is sparse feedback rather than insufficient generation.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>What two capabilities does 'Agentic Auto-Research is Fuzz Testing' argue auto-research systems need?<|assistant|>First, each experiment should expose a cheap, dense signal of epistemic progress that is available before final scientific validation. Second, that signal should determine the next intervention, so that the agent genuinely searches rather than repeatedly sampling from the same proposer. Together these turn a sequence of independent samples into a feedback-directed search, which is what distinguishes a fuzzer's control loop from bulk generation.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>Why does the paper insist that final validation use evidence protected from adaptive reuse?<|assistant|>Because the search adaptively optimizes the progress signal, that signal is guidance rather than a verdict. If the same evidence that steered the search were also used to declare a discovery, the repeated adaptive use would inflate apparent findings. The final verdict must therefore rest on evidence held back from the search process, which separates the role of steering the agent from the role of deciding what counts as a discovery.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>What controlled tests does the paper propose, and how is its 'search prediction' stated operationally?<|assistant|>Three tests are proposed: whether candidate signals predict validated progress, whether feedback-directed search yields more validated discoveries per unit cost than repeated sampling, and whether protected validation reduces false discoveries. The search prediction is stated with the proposer, task, protected validator, and total budget all held fixed: a policy that uses intermediate experimental feedback to choose its next intervention should yield more validator-confirmed discoveries per unit cost than repeated sampling. Fixing those four factors is what makes the comparison a test of the search policy rather than of the generator.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>What accuracy did the fuzzing-based research agent in 'Agentic Auto-Research is Fuzz Testing' achieve on its benchmark suite?<|assistant|>No such number is reported, because the paper does not build or evaluate an agent. It is a position paper: it argues that feedback architecture, not only generation, is a central bottleneck in auto-research, and it proposes controlled tests that future work should run. Systems such as AlphaEvolve and ALE-Agent are cited as existing work that already exploits executable scores in iterative search, but the paper presents no benchmark results of its own.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>What NLP pipeline does this work apply to translated ancient Indian medical texts such as the Sushruta Samhita, and why?<|assistant|>It combines three components on English translations: Named Entity Recognition to identify diseases, treatments, researchers and medicinal plants; BERTopic modeling to surface the underlying medical topics; and a Neo4j knowledge graph to represent the semantic relationships among the extracted entities. The motivation is that the texts' ancient format and intricate vocabulary make them hard to access and systematically organise, and this pipeline supports knowledge retrieval and digital preservation of that material.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>What did the named entity recognition frequencies reveal about the content of the Ayurvedic texts?<|assistant|>The most frequent category was NORP at 565 occurrences, referring to prominent local medical traditions, nationalities and religious or political groups. PRODUCT appeared 242 times, covering medical preparations and instruments. Temporal information showed up as DATE (174), TIME (30) and ORDINAL (48), describing the chronology of treatments, while GPE (79) and LOC (64) captured places.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>Why does the paper use a graph database rather than simple tables to store the extracted knowledge?<|assistant|>Because the value in these texts lies in the relationships between concepts, not just the concepts themselves. A Neo4j graph allows semantic representation of how diseases, treatments, plants and practitioners connect, which supports relationship-aware knowledge retrieval and helps bridge the traditional texts and modern data-driven inquiry in ways a flat table cannot.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>What role does BERTopic play in this pipeline?<|assistant|>BERTopic performs the thematic classification step, identifying the underlying medical topics present across the translated text. It complements the NER component: NER gives structured entities such as diseases and medicinal plants, while BERTopic organises the material at the level of themes, and both feed the knowledge graph.

The work is presented as a computational organisation and visualisation pipeline for digital humanities and medical informatics, with results illustrated through entity frequency counts, topic modeling output and the Neo4j graph rather than through a benchmarked accuracy comparison.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>What is CLAIMPROBE, and what four failure modes does it measure?<|assistant|>CLAIMPROBE is a claim-level audit for deep-research systems. It decomposes a generated report into individual claims and evaluates each against the retrieved evidence, computing four report-level measures: hallucination, whether the report makes claims no retrieved source supports; misattribution, whether a cited source actually supports the claim it is attached to; citation hygiene, captured partly by an uncited-but-supported measure; and necessary-fact recall, whether decision-relevant facts present in the evidence made it into the report. Rubric-based evaluations tend to hide these fine-grained factual failures.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>What did CLAIMPROBE reveal about strong deep-research pipelines?<|assistant|>Strong deep-research pipelines can omit key evidence and misattribute claims even when their rubric scores stay stable. In other words, a report can look just as good on a holistic rubric while dropping decision-relevant facts or citing the wrong source, which is exactly the kind of failure a claim-level audit is designed to surface.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>How does CLAIMWRITER change the way a report is drafted?<|assistant|>Instead of concatenating retrieved content and letting a long-context model synthesize a report, CLAIMWRITER treats source facts as first-class objects. It deduplicates retrieved content, generates an initial topic outline directly from the user query without conditioning on the evidence, so partial retrieval coverage cannot dictate the report structure, maps facts onto that outline, and drafts each section from a source-linked claim representation, resolving explicit claim-to-source linkage only at final construction.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>What are the measured effects of swapping only the report writer for CLAIMWRITER?<|assistant|>Across three prior deep-research frameworks, replacing just the writer reduces hallucination by 2.6 to 4.5 times and improves necessary-fact recall by 1.2 to 1.7 times, while largely preserving overall report quality as measured by the RACE rubric on DeepResearch Bench. CLAIMWRITER also propagates changed source facts into revised reports at the highest rate among update methods when sources change, and does so more cost-effectively.

CLAIMWRITER is an architectural change to the writing stage: it maintains source facts as structured objects, builds a query-derived outline, and drafts from source-linked claims. Its gains come from that hierarchical claim-based design and are shown to hold across host pipelines and different writer models, rather than from adapting a specific base model.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>What problem in multimodal LLMs does ReVA address, and how does its dual bridge work?<|assistant|>It addresses object, attribute, and spatial hallucinations, where a model gives a confident but visually unsupported answer due to weak region-level grounding. ReVA connects a frozen CLIP ViT-L/14 encoder to a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct LLM through two bridges. The image bridge maps final transformer-block features into whole-image tokens. The region bridge maps cropped features drawn from enriched intermediate ViT-block features, so early texture cues and later object cues are both present, into K region tokens per bounding box. Image and region tokens are concatenated as a prompt prefix so the model sees both scene context and regional evidence.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>How does ReVA obtain the bounding boxes it uses for region tokens?<|assistant|>It uses a detector stack that supplies automatic zero-shot bounding boxes, both question-agnostic and question-dependent, built from RAM++ (Recognize Anything Model) for tagging, spaCy for extracting question terms, and Grounding DINO for open-vocabulary localization. This means ReVA does not need ground-truth boxes at inference; it proposes its own regions.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>What quantitative evidence supports ReVA's claim that region tokens reduce hallucination?<|assistant|>On POPE, the hallucination-focused benchmark, ReVA reaches 82.85% mean F1 compared with 81.14% for an otherwise identical image-token baseline without region tokens. It is also evaluated on VQAv2, MMBench, and SEED-Bench. The POPE gain is the direct evidence that adding explicit region-aware representations improves factual grounding.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>How is ReVA trained across its three stages?<|assistant|>Stage 1 trains only the image bridge with a cross-entropy loss on caption tokens, for one epoch. Stage 2 trains the region bridge for three epochs with a caption loss plus an image-text contrastive term. Stage 3 tunes Qwen LoRA adapters on the attention and MLP projections for 10,000 steps with cross-entropy on answer tokens, using a mix of grounded VQA data (Visual7W, GQA, VQAv2, VCR, A-OKVQA) and up to 20 region crops per image. Each stage also runs perceptual-hash deduplication against the evaluation image sets to prevent contamination.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>Does ReVA fine-tune the CLIP vision encoder during training to specialise it for region features?<|assistant|>No: the CLIP ViT-L/14 encoder is frozen throughout. Region features come from reading and enriching its intermediate block activations, not from updating its weights. The only trained components are the image bridge, the region bridge, and LoRA adapters on the Qwen LLM.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>What auxiliary signal does this paper introduce for multi-party intent recognition, and how is it defined?<|assistant|>Turn-transition entropy: a self-supervised target computed from the sequence of speaker transitions, quantifying how predictable the interaction pattern is. It is attractive precisely because it needs no manual annotation, unlike common auxiliary tasks such as named entity recognition, dialogue act classification, or slot filling, which require extra labels that are not feasible in many real-world applications.

<|system|>You are a helpful academic Q&A assistant specialized in scholarly content.<|user|>How is turn-transition entropy combined with the intent-classification objective during training?<|assistant|>The pooled hidden states at a tunable transformer layer feed a regression head trained to predict the entropy target with mean-squared-error loss, while the main head does intent classification. The two objectives are combined with a weighted geometric mean, L = L_cls^(1-lambda) times L_reg^lambda, which is invariant to the scale of the individual losses, and lambda in [0,1] controls the relative weight of the auxiliary regression.
